results.description: The model update is X^{t+1} = X^t + γ H^t (W - I) - η V^t (Algorithm 1, line 3).
results.evidence: beer_repro/algorithms.py, line 36: `self.x += self.gamma * ((self.w - np.eye(self.w.shape[0])) @ self.h) - self.lr * self.v`. Line 35 comments: `# X^{t+1}=X^t+gamma(W-I)H^t-eta V^t`. This directly implements X^{t+1} = X^t + γ(W-I)H^t - η V^t, which is the formula in Algorithm 1 line 3 (γ maps to `self.gamma`, η to `self.lr`, H^t to `self.h`, V^t to `self.v`, W to `self.w`).
results.note: The code uses row-major layout so the matrix product order is `(W-I) @ H` rather than `H(W-I)`, but these are equivalent for this symmetric update in decentralized optimization — standard convention difference only.

results.description: The algorithm compresses the difference between the updated model and the previous surrogate: Q_h^{t+1} = C(X^{t+1} - H^t) (Algorithm 1, line 4).
results.evidence: beer_repro/algorithms.py lines 37-41: after updating self.x (= X^{t+1}) on line 36, the code computes `qh[i] = compress(self.x[i] - self.h[i], ...)` for each client i, where self.h is H^t (the surrogate). This is exactly Q_h^{t+1} = C(X^{t+1} - H^t). The surrogate is then updated via `self.h += qh` (H^{t+1} = H^t + Q_h^{t+1}).
results.note: The variable names qh/self.h/self.x map directly to Q_h^{t+1}, H^t, X^{t+1} from Algorithm 1. The comment on line 35 also references the X^{t+1} update formula, confirming the paper mapping.

results.description: The compressed surrogate H^t is updated as H^{t+1} = H^t + Q_h^{t+1} (Algorithm 1, line 5).
results.evidence: In `beer_repro/algorithms.py`, the BEER class `step` method computes `qh[i] = compress(self.x[i] - self.h[i], ...)` for each client, then updates `self.h += qh` (line ~43). This directly implements H^{t+1} = H^t + Q_h^{t+1}, where `self.h` is H^t and `qh` is the compressed quantity Q_h^{t+1}. The comment on the preceding line also marks the X update as `X^{t+1}=X^t+gamma(W-I)H^t-eta V^t`, confirming this is Algorithm 1.
results.note: The code uses row-major layout (n clients by d params), so `self.h` is a 2D array, but the update pattern per-row matches the described formula exactly.

results.description: The gradient estimate update uses gradient tracking: V^{t+1} = V^t + γ G^t (W - I) + ∇̃_b F(X^{t+1}) - ∇̃_b F(X^t) (Algorithm 1, line 6).
results.evidence: In beer_repro/algorithms.py, the BEER.step() method contains the line: `self.v += self.gamma * ((self.w - np.eye(self.w.shape[0])) @ self.g) + gradients - self.grad_previous`. This directly implements V^{t+1} = V^t + γ G^t (W-I) + ∇̃_b F(X^{t+1}) - ∇̃_b F(X^t), where self.v=V, self.gamma=γ, self.g=G^t (compressed gradient tracker), (self.w - np.eye(...)) @ self.g applies (W-I) to G^t, `gradients` is the new stochastic gradient, and `self.grad_previous` is the previous-step gradient.
results.note: The matrix multiplication order appears as (W-I) @ G (left-multiply) but due to the row-major layout (n clients × d params), this is equivalent to G^t(W-I) in the paper's column-vector notation.

results.description: The algorithm compresses the difference between the updated gradient estimate and the previous surrogate: Q_g^{t+1} = C(V^{t+1} - G^t) (Algorithm 1, line 7).
results.evidence: In beer_repro/algorithms.py, the BEER.step() method (lines ~50-55) computes: `qg[i] = compress(self.v[i] - self.g[i], ...)` for each client i, then `self.g += qg`. Here `self.v` holds the updated gradient estimate V^{t+1} (updated just above), `self.g` holds the previous surrogate G^t, and the compressed difference `compress(self.v[i] - self.g[i])` matches Q_g^{t+1} = C(V^{t+1} - G^t) exactly.

results.description: The compressed surrogate G^t is updated as G^{t+1} = G^t + Q_g^{t+1} (Algorithm 1, line 8).
results.evidence: In beer_repro/algorithms.py, lines 43-45 of the BEER.step() method: `qg[i] = compress(self.v[i] - self.g[i], ...)` computes Q_g^{t+1} for each client, then `self.g += qg` implements G^{t+1} = G^t + Q_g^{t+1}. The variable `self.g` is initialized to zeros (line 20) and accumulates compressed quantizations exactly as described in Algorithm 1, line 8.
results.note: The variable names match the paper: `self.g` = G^t (compressed surrogate), `qg` = Q_g^{t+1} (compressed correction). The update rule is applied row-by-row (per client) and then accumulated into `self.g`.

results.description: The algorithm initializes H^0 = 0 and G^0 = 0 (Algorithm 1, line 1).
results.evidence: beer_repro/algorithms.py, lines 19-20: `self.h = np.zeros_like(self.x)` and `self.g = np.zeros_like(self.x)` in BEER.__init__. These initialize H^0 and G^0 to zero arrays matching the shape of x, exactly as Algorithm 1 line 1 requires.

results.description: V^0 is initialized to the full gradient ∇F(X^0) (Algorithm 1, line 1).
results.evidence: In beer_repro/runner.py lines 72-79, V^0 is initialized via `alg.initialize(initial_gradients)` where `initial_gradients` is computed using `client.batch(0, cfg["batch_size"])` — a mini-batch of size `batch_size`, NOT the full gradient over all training data. The algorithms.py `initialize` method (lines 26-29) sets `self.v = gradients.copy()` correctly, but receives mini-batch gradients rather than the full ∇F(X^0). The paper's Algorithm 1, line 1 specifies V^0 = ∇F(X^0), where ∇F denotes the full gradient summed over all data points.
results.note: The initialization structure itself is correct (V^0 is explicitly set before training at X^0), but it uses stochastic/mini-batch gradients instead of the full gradient. This is a meaningful algorithmic discrepancy from what Algorithm 1 line 1 prescribes.

results.description: X^0 is initialized such that all clients start with the same initial point x^0, i.e., X^0 = x^0 1^⊤ (Algorithm 1, line 1).
results.evidence: beer_repro/runner.py line 69: `x0 = np.tile(_initial_params(cfg["task"], data_info["features"], seed), (clients, 1))`. This creates a 2-D array of shape (clients, d) by tiling a single initial parameter vector (returned by `_initial_params`) across all `clients` rows, so every client starts at the exact same point — implementing X^0 = x^0 * 1^⊤.
results.note: The `np.tile(..., (clients, 1))` call broadcasts the single shared vector x^0 to all n clients, matching Algorithm 1 line 1 exactly.

results.description: The gradient oracle used in the update is a minibatch stochastic gradient ∇̃_b F(X) with minibatch size b (Algorithm 1, line 6).
results.evidence: beer_repro/data.py lines 16-21: ClientData.batch(round_id, batch_size) draws a contiguous minibatch of size batch_size. beer_repro/runner.py line 84: batch_data = [client.batch(round_id, cfg["batch_size"]) for client in client_data]; lines 86-91: for each client i, loss, grad = grad_fn(point, bx, by) computes the gradient on that minibatch; grads = np.asarray(grads) is the per-client stochastic gradient array passed to alg.step(grads). All experiment configs set "batch_size": 100 (e.g. configs/exp_001_a9a_comparison.json line 9).
results.note: The minibatch size b is the config key "batch_size"; gradients are computed per-client on a batch of that size before being passed into the algorithm step, matching Algorithm 1 line 6.

results.evidence: configs/exp_001_a9a_comparison.json: "clients": 10, "topology": "ring", "task": "a9a". beer_repro/data.py load_a9a() (lines 37-61): data is sorted by label (np.argsort, stable), then split via _partition() which calls np.array_split(np.arange(len(labels)), clients) — producing 10 even contiguous chunks. graphs.py implements ring topology connecting n nodes in a cycle. results.description: Approximately, for the `a9a` dataset, 5 clients receive data with label 1 and others receive data with label 0.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/data.py, load_a9a() sorts training samples by label (np.argsort) and then splits into 10 contiguous chunks. The a9a dataset has ~24% positive (+1) and ~76% negative (-1) samples (32561 total, ~7841 positive). After sorting and splitting into 10 equal chunks of ~3256: clients 0-7 receive label=-1 data (7 clients entirely negative, client 7 mixed), and only clients 8-9 receive label=+1 data. This means approximately 2 clients receive positive-label data, not 5. Furthermore, the labels in the code are -1 and +1 (not 0 and 1). The configs/exp_001_a9a_comparison.json confirms 10 clients are used.
results.note: The claim may be describing a different partition scheme (e.g., 5 clients with one class and 5 with another for a balanced split), but the actual implementation produces ~2 clients with label +1 and ~8 with label -1, due to the a9a dataset's class imbalance (~24% positive).

results.description: The objective function is logistic regression with a nonconvex regularizer: f(x; (a, b)) = log(1 + exp(-b a^T x)) + α ∑_{j=1}^d x_j^2 / (1 + x_j^2), with regularization parameter α = 0.05.
results.evidence: beer_repro/objectives.py, function `logistic_loss_gradient` (lines 8-14): loss = np.logaddexp(0.0, -margin).mean() + alpha * np.sum(params * params / (1.0 + params * params)), with default alpha=0.05. This exactly matches f(x;(a,b)) = log(1+exp(-b·aᵀx)) + α∑xⱼ²/(1+xⱼ²) with α=0.05.
results.note: The gradient is also correctly implemented: grad += alpha * 2.0 * params / (1.0 + params * params) ** 2, which is the derivative of the nonconvex regularizer.

results.description: The mixing matrix is the FDLA matrix (Xiao and Boyd, 2004).
results.evidence: beer_repro/graphs.py line 37-49 defines `mixing_matrix()` with docstring "Return a symmetric, doubly stochastic Metropolis matrix with self-loops." The weight formula used is `1.0 / (1.0 + max(deg[i], deg[j]))`, which is the Metropolis-Hastings rule, not the FDLA matrix. There is no reference to FDLA, Xiao, or Boyd anywhere in the Python source files. The experiment config configs/exp_001_a9a_comparison.json sets `"topology": "ring"` but does not specify any FDLA matrix computation.
results.note: The FDLA matrix requires solving a semidefinite program to find the fastest-converging mixing matrix for a given graph topology. The code instead uses the simpler Metropolis-Hastings weighting rule, which is a different (suboptimal) mixing matrix.

results.description: The 10 clients are connected by a ring topology, and the FDLA mixing matrix (Xiao and Boyd, 2004) is used.

The actual spectral gap measured in the formal run is 0.5421698984578338 (results/formal/exp_003_a9a_topology/metrics.json, key "spectral_gap"; also confirmed in run.log: "spectral_gap=0.54216990"). This is a stochastic graph, so the value is seed/instance-dependent, but the repository's recorded value is definitively not 0.51.

results.evidence: The formal experiment exp_003_a9a_topology ran ER topology with p=0.5 (40 clients), recording spectral_gap=0.54217 (run.log line 1: "topology=er spectral_gap=0.54216990"). CLAIM_RESULTS.json confirms "Erdos-Renyi p=0.5 run is successful, records spectral gap 0.54217." results.description: The evaluation metrics reported are the training gradient norm and testing accuracy.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/runner.py, the metrics dict is initialized with keys "gradient_norm" and "test_accuracy" for each method (line: `metrics = {name: {"round": [], "gradient_norm": [], "test_accuracy": [], ...}}`). After each round, gradient_norm is computed as `np.linalg.norm(eval_grad)` (the training gradient norm at the averaged model) and test_accuracy via `acc_fn(avg, test.features, test.labels)`. A comment reads "The paper reports a training gradient norm." The plotting loop explicitly uses ylabel "training gradient norm" and "test accuracy" for the two figures. Config exp_003_a9a_topology.json targets a9a dataset with methods:["BEER"], matching the verification spec exp3_topology_a9a/BEER/a9a.
results.note: The experiment config is exp_003_a9a_topology (not exp3_topology_a9a, but clearly the same experiment). Both metrics are fully implemented.

results.description: The experiment uses the unshuffled `a9a` dataset split evenly to 40 agents.
results.evidence: configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json sets "clients": 10, not 40. results/formal/exp_004_a9a_compression/resolved_config.json confirms "clients": 10. Additionally, beer_repro/data.py's load_a9a() explicitly sorts the data by label before partitioning (order = np.argsort(train_y, kind="stable"); train_x, train_y = train_x[order], train_y[order]) rather than using the unshuffled original order.
results.note: Two conditions fail: (1) 10 agents not 40, and (2) data is label-sorted not unshuffled.

results.description: The objective is logistic regression with nonconvex regularization with regularization parameter α = 0.05.
results.evidence: beer_repro/objectives.py: `logistic_loss_gradient(params, features, labels, alpha=0.05)` computes logistic loss plus `alpha * np.sum(params * params / (1.0 + params * params))` — a nonconvex regularizer — with default alpha=0.05. configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json explicitly sets `"alpha": 0.05` for the BEER experiment on the a9a dataset.
results.note: The regularizer p²/(1+p²) is a classic nonconvex penalty (bounded, concave for large |p|), consistent with the paper's §5.2 description.

results.description: The network topology is a ring topology.
results.evidence: configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json contains "topology": "ring" for experiment_id "exp_004_a9a_compression", method BEER, dataset a9a.

results.description: The batch size b is 100 for all compression schemes.
results.evidence: configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json line 9: "batch_size": 100. This config covers all compression schemes for the a9a experiment (exp4). Confirmed by results/formal/exp_004_a9a_compression/resolved_config.json line 3: "batch_size": 100. The runner uses cfg["batch_size"] uniformly across all methods (beer_repro/runner.py lines 74 and 84), so BEER and all other compression schemes use batch size 100.

results.description: For BEER with no compression or gsgd5 compression, the step size η is 0.5.
results.evidence: configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json (the config for exp4_compression_a9a) sets "lr": 0.5 for BEER. The runner (beer_repro/runner.py, _make_algorithm function) passes cfg["lr"] directly as the step size to BEER: `BEER(x0, gamma=cfg["gamma"], ..., lr=cfg["lr"], ...)`. This single lr=0.5 applies to all compression variants in the experiment, including no compression (identity) and gsgd5.
results.note: The config specifies a single lr=0.5 for the entire experiment. The compression type (no compression, gsgd5, top_k, etc.) does not change the step size — there is no per-variant lr override logic.

results.description: For BEER with top10 compression, the step size η is 0.005.
results.evidence: In configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json and results/formal/exp_004_a9a_compression/resolved_config.json, the step size is "lr": 0.5 (not 0.005). The BEER algorithm in beer_repro/algorithms.py uses self.lr directly as η (line 36: `self.x += self.gamma * ((self.w - np.eye(...)) @ self.h) - self.lr * self.v`). The config specifies compression_param=10 (top10) and method=BEER, but lr=0.5, contradicting the claim that η=0.005.
results.note: The value 0.005 does not appear anywhere in the repository configs or algorithm code for BEER with top10 compression on a9a.

results.evidence: configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json sets "gamma": 0.7 for the BEER method on the a9a compression experiment. The resolved_config.json at results/formal/exp_004_a9a_compression/resolved_config.json confirms "gamma": 0.7. The runner (beer_repro/runner.py line 33) passes cfg["gamma"] directly to BEER, so this single gamma value of 0.7 applies to all compression variants in that experiment including no compression (identity) and gsgd5.

results.description: The compression schemes compared are no compression, gsgd5, and top10.
results.evidence: The experiment config at configs/exp_004_a9a_compression.json defines only a single compressor variant: "compressor": "top" with "compression_param": 10 (i.e., top10). The "methods" field contains only ["BEER"] — there is no sweep or multi-variant comparison. The runner.py does not implement any sweep over compression types; it reads one config and runs one configuration. No config or script exists that compares "no compression" (identity), "gsgd5", and "top10" in a single experiment. CLAIM_RESULTS.json (line ~39-44) explicitly notes: "a complete same-bit sweep across all Figure 4 operators is not asserted." All three operators (identity, gsgd, top_k) are implemented in compression.py but they are not compared together in exp4_compression_a9a.
results.note: The paper's §5.2 Figure 4 shows a comparison of multiple compression schemes, but the repository's exp_004_a9a_compression only implements a single run with top10 compression. The rubric's specific claim of comparing no compression + gsgd5 + top10 is not implemented.

results.description: The first module of the CNN consists of a 2-d convolution layer with 1 input channel, 16 output channels, kernel size 5, stride 1, and padding 2, followed by 2-d batch normalization, ReLU activation, and 2-d max pooling with kernel size 2 and stride 2.
results.evidence: The MNIST model is implemented in beer_repro/objectives.py as a 2-layer MLP with sigmoid activation: nn_loss_gradient uses `z1 = features @ w1.T + b1` (linear layer, hidden=32) then sigmoid, then a second linear layer. There is no CNN, no Conv2d, no BatchNorm2d, no ReLU, and no MaxPool2d anywhere in the codebase. The runner.py confirms "Xavier initialization for the 32-neuron, 784-input network" for MNIST. No PyTorch or any deep learning framework is imported.
results.note: The experiment uses a simple MLP, not the CNN architecture described in the rubric. The rubric references "exp5_cnn_mnist" but the repo has no CNN implementation at all.

results.description: The second module of the CNN is the same as the first module, except the convolution layer has 16 input channels and 32 output channels.
results.evidence: The MNIST model is implemented in beer_repro/objectives.py as a 2-layer fully-connected MLP (nn_unpack, nn_loss_gradient, nn_accuracy). It uses dense weight matrices w1 (hidden×input_dim) and w2 (classes×hidden) with sigmoid activations — no convolutional layers, no "modules", no channel dimensions anywhere. The runner.py initializes it as a flat parameter vector. Grep for "CNN", "Conv", "conv", "channel" across all .py files returns no matches relevant to a CNN architecture. The exp5_cnn_mnist experiment_id does not exist in configs either (only exp_001 through exp_005 exist, and exp_005 is MNIST heterogeneity with the MLP).
results.note: The paper apparently describes a CNN for section 5.3, but the reproduction uses only a simple MLP for MNIST experiments. No CNN with any convolutional layers is implemented.

results.description: The last module of the CNN is a fully-connected layer with 1568 inputs and 10 outputs.
results.evidence: Searched all .py and .json files for CNN-related keywords (1568, CNN, Conv, cnn, conv2d, MaxPool, fully-connected, Linear) and found no CNN implementation. The only neural network in the codebase is in beer_repro/objectives.py: a two-layer sigmoid network (nn_loss_gradient / nn_unpack) with 32 hidden units and no convolutional layers. No experiment matching "exp5_cnn_mnist" exists — only "exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity" which uses the simple sigmoid network. The value 1568 does not appear as any layer dimension anywhere in the code.
results.note: The repository does not implement a CNN at all for any experiment. The MNIST experiments use a 32-hidden-unit fully-connected sigmoid network, not a convolutional architecture.

results.description: The loss function is the standard cross-entropy loss.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/objectives.py, function `nn_loss_gradient` (used for MNIST experiments) computes softmax probabilities and then applies cross-entropy: `loss = -np.log(np.maximum(probs[np.arange(len(labels)), labels], 1e-12)).mean()`. This is standard cross-entropy loss. In runner.py, for task=="mnist", the grad_fn is set to `nn_loss_gradient`, confirming it's used for exp5 (exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity).
results.note: The rubric mentions "CNN" but the actual implementation uses a two-layer fully connected MLP (not a CNN). However, the loss function itself is standard cross-entropy as claimed.

results.description: Each agent's model is simply averaged with its neighbors.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/algorithms.py, DSGD.step() does `self.x = self.w @ self.x - self.lr * gradients`. The mixing matrix W is constructed in beer_repro/graphs.py mixing_matrix() as a Metropolis doubly-stochastic matrix where off-diagonal weights are `1.0 / (1.0 + max(deg[i], deg[j]))` — not equal averaging weights. For a ring topology (used in exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity), each node has degree 2, so each off-diagonal weight is 1/3 and self-weight is 1/3, which happens to look like equal averaging. However, the implementation uses a general weighted Metropolis scheme, not "simple averaging." The `BEER` algorithm (also included in the methods list for exp5) uses a more complex update: `self.x += self.gamma * ((self.w - I) @ self.h) - self.lr * self.v`, which is clearly not simple averaging. No code path implements "simply averaging each agent's model with its neighbors" as a standalone operation.
results.note: For a ring topology specifically (used in exp_005), the Metropolis weights do yield equal weights of 1/3 for self+2 neighbors, which is effectively a simple average. However, BEER's update rule is fundamentally different from simple averaging, and the claim applies to "all" methods. The claim as stated does not match BEER's algorithm which uses compressed gradient tracking, not simple model averaging.

results.description: Both BEER and CHOCO-SGD employ the biased gsgd_b compression with b=5.
results.evidence: The MNIST heterogeneity experiment (exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity.json / resolved_config.json) uses compressor="identity" with compression_param=0, and only includes methods ["BEER", "DSGD"] — CHOCO-SGD is absent. The only MNIST config that includes both BEER and CHOCO-SGD is exp_002_mnist_comparison.json, which uses compressor="gsgd" with compression_param=20 (not b=5). The b=5 gsgd configuration only appears in exp_001_a9a_comparison.json and exp_003_a9a_topology.json, both for the a9a dataset, not MNIST.
results.note: The claim requires both BEER and CHOCO-SGD to use gsgd_b with b=5 on unshuffled MNIST (exp5_cnn_mnist). No such configuration exists: the unshuffled MNIST experiment uses identity compression and omits CHOCO-SGD entirely.

results.description: The dataset is the unshuffled MNIST dataset.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/data.py, the load_mnist() function reads train.parquet and test.parquet files and does NOT perform any shuffle operation. The entire codebase has zero occurrences of "shuffle" (grep confirmed). The data is loaded as-is (unshuffled) and partitioned by label (by_label=True, one digit per client). The config exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity.json (experiment_id matching exp5_cnn_mnist) confirms MNIST is the dataset used.
results.note: The exp5 config uses experiment_id "exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity" which maps to the CNN/MNIST heterogeneity experiment in Section 5.3. The absence of any shuffle call confirms the data remains in its original (unshuffled) order.

results.description: Testing gradient norm and testing accuracy are evaluated against communication bits.
results.evidence: In beer_repro/runner.py, the metrics dict tracks "communication_bits" (line: metrics[name]["communication_bits"].append(int(alg.bits))), but the plotting loop uses "round" as the x-axis for both gradient_norm and test_accuracy figures: `ax.plot(values["round"], values[field], label=name)` with `ax.set_xlabel("communication rounds")`. There is no plot or figure generated that uses communication_bits as the x-axis against gradient_norm or test_accuracy. The exp_005_mnist_heterogeneity config targets the relevant experiment (MNIST, BEER+DSGD), but the figures produced plot metrics vs. rounds, not vs. communication bits as described in the paper's Figure 5.
results.note: The communication_bits data IS collected per round, but is never used as an x-axis in any generated figure. The rubric specifically requires evaluation "against communication bits" (i.e., x-axis = bits), which the implementation does not do.
